claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered single-phase BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
The limited plasticity of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is caused by the electronegativity difference associated with its high Mo content.
Replacing half of the Mo with V to form NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5 reduces the overall electronegativity difference in the BCC matrix.
Atomic-size mismatch and electronegativity mismatch are factors affecting solid-solution stability and intrinsic properties in high-entropy alloys.
Lower electronegativity mismatch can correspond to a more stable electronic and solid-solution state.
V has lower electronegativity than Mo.
Reducing Mo content diminishes localized bond stiffening associated with high electronegativity contrast.
Incorporating V moderates lattice distortion in NbZrTiHfMo-based alloys.
V substitution maintains solid-solution strengthening through atomic-size mismatch.
Reduced electronegativity contrast and moderated lattice distortion improve dislocation mobility.
NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5 will exhibit a 20–30% increase in room-temperature compressive plastic strain relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5 will retain a room-temperature compressive yield strength near 1650–1700 MPa.
Arc melting, homogenization at about 1600°C, and controlled cooling can retain a disordered single-phase BCC structure in the modified alloy.
The beneficial strength–plasticity effect is conditional on retention of the single-phase disordered BCC structure.
Excessive Mo-to-V substitution may cause phase instability or secondary-phase formation.
A composition series from x = 0 to x = 1, including an x = 0 control, will be tested by phase characterization and room-temperature compression.
Failure to achieve at least a 20% statistically significant plastic-strain increase while retaining 1650–1700 MPa yield strength is designated as a falsifying outcome.

contradictions.description: The boundary anticipates secondary phases when substitution exceeds an unknown optimum, but the experiment includes compositions through complete substitution and the rule could treat secondary phases in any tested alloy as falsification. Secondary phases at an explicitly out-of-bound composition therefore risk being counted against a hypothesis that is stated not to apply there.
